chapter_note: This chapter is dominated by later dialogical/pastoral material about anger, reprimand, repentance, and conduct among ‘brothers/sisters’, wrapped in Kephalaia-style Q&A frame. A single brief cosmological-correspondential fragment (¶9) grounds the ethical ‘two aspects’ (love/fear) in the heavenly light-givers’ purificatory function; it stays entirely within the cosmic system and reads like an older teaching insert. An NT paraphrase (Mt 6:21) appears in ¶10, marking Christian overlay there.

paragraphs.temporal_note: Opens with formulaic Kephalaia dialogue frame (“Once again… disciple… says to him: I beseech you…”). The question concerns practical dealings with ‘brother or sister’ and ‘judgement… righteousness’, i.e., community ethics rather than cosmological system exposition.

First-person practical resolve about using anger to subdue someone ‘with righteous judgement’; no cosmological mapping, framed as community discipline/application rather than impersonal system teaching.
Q&A petition formula (“I beseech you, my master, that you may instruct me… whether there is sin…”) typical of the editorial dialogue apparatus; content is moral casuistry, not cosmic structure.

Contains explicit dialogue attribution (“Then the apostle speaks…”) and proceeds with disciplinary counsel about ‘repentance’, ‘rebuke’, ‘censure’, ‘upbraid’—institutional/ethical application rather than cosmos→cosmos correspondential description.
Extended ethical taxonomy of ‘evil anger’ (pride, abuse, cursing, retaliation) and interpersonal conflict among ‘brothers’; lacks impersonal cosmological mechanics and functions as moral instruction.
Community disciplinary guidance (“strong reprimand that leads to repentance”); no cosmic register. Reads as institutional pastoral teaching.

Homiletic simile of the wise doctor using hot/cool remedies. This is illustrative rhetoric supporting ethical instruction, not a systematic cosmos→cosmos mapping characteristic of the oldest substrate.
Applies the doctor simile directly to speaking with people in ‘two aspects’ (love/fear) to overcome ‘obduracy’ and bring repentance; remains practical/disciplinary and audience-oriented.

paragraphs.core_text: For the light-givers that are in the heavens shall be revealed with these two aspects, in the aspect of love and the aspect of fear. They display these two aspects of the powers above that are in the heavens, because of their soul that passes through the totality. For in these two appearances, the aspect of love that is beauty and sublimity, together with the other aspect of confrontation that is in them, they shall purify in them the powers above.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Impersonal cosmological-correspondential statement: heavenly ‘light-givers’ manifest two aspects (love/fear) and purify ‘the powers above’ due to ‘their soul that passes through the totality’. Both sides of the mapping remain within the cosmic system (no contemporary institutions/audience address), marking it as an older teaching fragment embedded in a later ethical discourse.

Direct exhortation (“you too”) culminating in an NT/Gospel paraphrase (“wherever your heart… your treasure…” ~ Mt 6:21). Because this language enters via the Gospel tradition, the paragraph is classified as Christian overlay.
Closing reaction formula (“When that teacher heard… he said… my master…”) typical of Kephalaia hagiographic/dialogue framing rather than core teaching.
